---
title: "Beyond the step test: MLSS and VLamax"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

Two tests answer what a step test cannot. Constant-load bouts give the maximal lactate steady state (MLSS), which the
second threshold tries to estimate, and a short sprint gives the maximal lactate accumulation rate (V̇La<sub>max</sub>).

## The maximal lactate steady state (MLSS)

The MLSS is the highest constant intensity at which blood lactate stays steady. Measure it with bouts of at least 30
min at different intensities, on separate days, sampling lactate at least at minutes 10 and 30: a bout is steady when
lactate rises by no more than 1 mmol/L from minute 10 to the end ([Beneke,
2003](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-002-0783-1)). The MLSS lies between the highest steady bout and the next bout up,
so bouts closer together pin it down better.

`lactate_mlss()` reads the bouts, one row per sample, and with the result of the step test it gives how far each
threshold lies from the MLSS:

```{r mlss, fig.height = 4.2}
bouts <- data.frame(
  intensity = rep(c(130, 140, 150), each = 4),
  time = rep(c(5, 10, 20, 30), 3),
  lactate = c(2.4, 2.6, 2.7, 2.8, 3.1, 3.4, 3.8, 4.1, 3.9, 4.5, 5.4, 6.3)
)
step_test <- lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity, lactate, plot = FALSE)
mlss <- lactate_mlss(bouts, step_test)
mlss
autoplot(mlss)
```

`mlss$thresholds` lists the gap of every threshold. In published studies the gap of a method ranged from about 2 to 49
W, depending on the protocol and the athletes (see [The methods and the evidence](methods.html#what-the-evidence-says)),
so the gaps over a group of your own athletes are the best answer to which threshold estimates the MLSS with your
protocol. Whether the MLSS is the boundary between the heavy and severe domains is debated: the critical power lies
12 W above it on average, with wide limits of agreement ([Micheli et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.19060);
[Jones et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.14098)).

## The maximal lactate accumulation rate (V̇La<sub>max</sub>)

V̇La<sub>max</sub> comes from its own test, a short all-out sprint, not from the step test:

$$\dot{V}\text{La}_{\text{max}} = \frac{\text{La}_{\text{peak}} - \text{La}_{\text{pre}}}{t_{\text{test}} - t_{\text{alactic}}}$$

Take a lactate sample before the sprint and every minute for several minutes after it; the highest value is the
peak. `vlamax()` does the arithmetic:

```{r}
vlamax(lactate_pre = 1.1, lactate_post = c(8.9, 10.4, 10.9, 10.6, 10.1), test_duration = 15)
```

The alactic time is the part of the sprint assumed to be covered by phosphocreatine. In 50 cyclists, fixing it at
3.5 s gave the most reliable V̇La<sub>max</sub> (ICC 0.91, CV 3.1%), while estimating it from the power curve did not (CV 12-26%);
a 1-s change in it can change V̇La<sub>max</sub> by up to 26% ([Meixner et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.16086)). Protocols differ widely between studies
([Langley et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.28985/1425.jsc.09)), and whether V̇La<sub>max</sub> measures the maximal glycolytic rate is still debated: in 11 cyclists it
added little beyond the power of the sprint itself ([Clark & Macdermid, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1080/02701367.2025.2481176)). Compare V̇La<sub>max</sub> only within the same
protocol, ergometer and analyzer.

`vlamax()` assumes a 15-s sprint by default, as in Meixner et al. (2024) and most cycling studies. A review of 60 studies
recommends a sport-specific all-out sprint of 10-12 s with lactate sampled every minute for 10 min, calls the rate
from 15 s or longer a peak rather than a maximal rate, and found the use of V̇La<sub>max</sub> to predict performances of 1 min
or longer inconclusive ([Quittmann, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-025-06022-7)). Give `test_duration` the length of your sprint.

`vlamax()` also returns vLa<sub>peak</sub>, the same rise divided by the whole sprint, with no alactic time, so it is
lower than V̇La<sub>max</sub>. [Wackerhage et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02259-6) proposed it, by analogy with V̇O<sub>2peak</sub>, partly because
the alactic-time correction is error-prone. In 182 cyclists and triathletes, both gave similar associations with the
lactate thresholds ([Röhrs et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-026-06444-x)).

## What the step test shows

Commercial software estimates V̇La<sub>max</sub> from submaximal bouts by fitting Mader's model of energy metabolism to the
lactate values. The only open description of the method we found is a preprint of 9 people, who did four
separate bouts with rest in between rather than a step test. Their V̇La<sub>max</sub> was never compared with a sprint, and the
authors note that the same power at the maximal lactate steady state may come from different mixes of V̇O<sub>2max</sub> and V̇La<sub>max</sub> ([Suttmeyer et al.,
2023](https://doi.org/10.51224/SRXIV.269)). The review above found that simulation approaches do not yet support predictions for an individual athlete
(Quittmann, 2026). Measure V̇La<sub>max</sub> with a sprint.

What the step test can show is its effect. At the same V̇O<sub>2max</sub>, Mader's model predicts that a higher V̇La<sub>max</sub> shifts
the lactate curve to the left (Wackerhage et al., 2025). In 50 cyclists, adding vLa<sub>peak</sub> to V̇O<sub>2max</sub> and sex explained
6 to 20 percentage points more of the variance in threshold power ([Meixner et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-026-06270-1)); in 182 cyclists and
triathletes it added about 5 points beyond V̇O<sub>2max</sub> and efficiency (Röhrs et al., 2026). In both, a higher rate went
with a lower threshold. So a curve that moved left while V̇O<sub>2max</sub> stayed the same may reflect a higher glycolytic rate,
not only lost endurance (see `curve_shape()`).
